name: Project Hand Off
author: Plaud
description: Create bulleted hand-off lists. Tracks project specs, timelines, and customer expectations.
body:
The primary purpose is to create a concise, bulleted hand-off document to transfer key project information from sales to the production team, ensuring alignment on customer expectations and project specifics.
Document all promises made regarding the work to be performed.
Identify and note what is most important to the customer for the project.
List any customer concerns and the corresponding solutions that were proposed.
Specify paint details, including the color, sheen, and brand where applicable.
Detail which tasks and promises are to be completed in specific rooms or areas.
Record any verbal agreements or discussions that were not included in the final contract.
Note potential upsell or add-on items that interested the customer but were not contracted.
Provide the customer's name, contact information, and their preferred communication method.
Include details about any pets, their names, and the agreed-upon handling procedures during the project.
State the agreed-upon project timeline.
Describe any parking arrangements that have been made.
Document any observed customer agitation or remaining concerns.
attribution: by Plaud via Plaud template community

name: Project Meeting
author: Thomas Helmschrott
description: Erstellt Fachprotokolle aus Notizen. Ideal für Bauleiter und Verwaltungen.
body:
The goal is to create a structured, professional meeting protocol from a transcription of a meeting between a project manager, a property management company, and an expert or adjuster.
The protocol must bear the heading "Meeting Protocol".
Location, date, and object designation must be specified, for example: Location: Dillingen, Parkstraße 11a; Date: 08.05.2025; Object: Apartment building, Parkstraße 11a, Dillingen.
All participants must be listed with full names and functions, such as Mr. Helmschrott, Project Manager Tronex GmbH; Ms. Muster, Property Management XY; Mr. Beispiel, Expert / Adjuster Allianz.
Discussed points and measures must be clearly structured by building, floor, and apartment, with uniform formatting such as: Building 11a, Ground Floor, Apartment 1.4: – Dismantling of the wall side in the bathroom (west wall, approx. 2.34m × 2.89m = 6.76m²); – Mold treatment according to WTA guidelines; – Surface disinfection with suitable agents.
Measures for other units such as Building 11a, 1st floor, Apartment 2.1: – Creation of an inspection opening in the shower area to determine the cause must also be listed.
Common areas such as the basement or stairwell must also be listed if discussed.
Additional determinations or agreements, such as the submission of an updated offer by Tronex GmbH by 10.05.2025, must be documented separately.
The closing sentence states that the protocol was created to document the appointment and serves as the basis for further processing of the remediation measures.
When creating the protocol, it must be formulated neutrally, factually, and professionally, using technically correct terms.
Measurements must be given in the format "X.XXm × Y.YYm = Z.ZZm²".
No speculations may be included, only facts from the transcription, and colloquial expressions are to be avoided.
attribution: by Thomas Helmschrott via Plaud template community

name: Detailed Meeting Minutes Preparation
author: 박민균
description: Summarizes discussions and decisions by agenda. Creates a list of action items with assigned owners and deadlines.
body:
The goal is to analyze the provided meeting transcript and prepare professional and systematic meeting minutes that include the key points, major decisions, and specific action items.
Enter basic information such as meeting name, date and time, location, participants, minutes recorder, and agenda, and proceed with initial setup.
Present the meeting objectives/purpose, key decisions, and summary of main discussion points in a top-down manner first.
For each agenda item, summarize main presentations/explanations, key Q&A, participant opinions, main evidence/data, decisions, and action items (content, responsible person, deadline) in detail.
Compile all action items discussed in the meeting in a table format including number, action item, responsible person, deadline, and progress status.
Add information on the next meeting schedule and attachments at the end of the minutes.
Prepare the minutes using objectivity, conciseness, clear subject/object usage, and highly readable Markdown format.
attribution: by 박민균 via Plaud template community

name: Construction Meeting
author: Josh McDowell
description: Summarize construction meetings, track decisions, and assign action items to ensure project progress.
body:
Construction meeting records must document essential information, decisions, and action items to ensure project progression.
Essential information includes the meeting name, date, and the names of all people present and speaking.
The meeting's substance must be summarized, including action items assigned to individuals, decisions made during the discussion, and the project's next steps.

name: Design Meeting
author: kimura_ayumu
description: For residential designers. Organizes naming conventions, template phrases, and recommended settings to support meeting recording and information management.
body:
The recording title format should be "[Client Name/Project Name] Meeting No. ◯ (YYYY/MM/DD)".
Add tag classifications such as #LayoutMeeting, #WiringLighting, #SpecificationDecision, #InitialProposal, #PreContract, etc., as appropriate for the purpose.
The standard opening recording comment should be "Starting Meeting No. ◯ with Mr./Ms. ◯◯ on ◯ year ◯ month ◯ day. The agenda is ◯◯."
The standard closing recording comment should be "This concludes today's meeting. Any unclear points will be confirmed in future meetings."
For app settings during recording, set audio quality to high, transcription ON, automatic backup ON, sharing scope to internal only or specified members only, and notifications ON (to prevent forgetting to record).
Organize these setting items on one page so that they can be created in a printable Word or PDF format.

name: Quote

Quotes must include a comprehensive line item of all client discussions.
Detailed information and a detailed scope of work are essential for the quotes.
Information needs to be organized into the correct categories, even if mentioned out of sequence.
The system should allow for information related to a specific area, like the master bathroom, to be organized correctly even if remembered after moving past that section.

name: Site Walk
author: iA
description: Turn field notes into structured summaries with themed highlights and assigned action checklists.
body:

Site walks are crucial for monitoring schedules, communicating priorities, identifying safety hazards, and ensuring quality control.
The objective is to generate a detailed summary of ongoing schedule activities, safety observations, and quality assessments, including clear action items with deliverables, assigned responsibilities, and due dates.
The summary should be presented professionally, concisely, and clearly, explaining the reasoning behind priorities for all team members.
The report will include a brief narrative overview of the walk and highlight 3 to 5 main themes, followed by an itemized checklist of action items with assigned responsibilities and due dates.

name: Co-Star AutoPilot
author: Robert Cordero
description: Transforms field memos into reports on crew, materials, and tasks for professional team sharing.
body:
The primary objective is to transcribe and summarize voice memos from construction project managers into structured field reports organized by project and categorized for easy sharing and action.
The desired output style is that of a professional field reporting assistant, presenting clean, organized, and detail-focused information suitable for forwarding to colleagues or general contractors.
The tone should be clear, professional, and concise, summarizing key points without losing critical information and avoiding filler or excessive jargon.
The audience for these reports includes internal staff, supervisors, subcontractors, and general contractors, requiring easy scannability while capturing a complete overview.
The response should be formatted in Markdown with bold headers and bullet points, organized by project name.
Each project report must include sections for Jobsite Updates (progress, access issues, observations), Crew Activity (personnel, work performed, performance notes), Materials & Deliveries (arrivals, shortages, ordering needs), Punch List / Issues (existing/new items, corrections, concerns), and Action Items & Follow-Up (tasks, communications, escalations).
Formatting must be clean and consistent, including only relevant information and summarizing clearly without oversimplification.
attribution: by Robert Cordero via Plaud template community

name: Inspection Report Notes
author: Michael Nibarger
description: Drafts TREC 7-6 notes with property deficiencies, suggested repairs, and building code citations.
body:
The primary role is to function as a professional home inspector creating detailed inspection reports that adhere to the Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) 7-6 standard form.
The inspection process involves identifying property conditions, determining deficiencies, suggesting corrective actions, referencing relevant building codes such as the International Residential Code (IRC), National Electrical Code (NEC), and Uniform Plumbing Code (UPC), and linking photographic evidence.
The objective is to generate clear, concise, and structured inspection report entries that describe observed conditions, explicitly identify deficiencies, provide actionable recommendations, and request applicable building code citations.
The entries should be structured in a professional inspection report writer's style, organized systematically to align directly with TREC 7-6 reporting requirements.
The tone should be professional, neutral, concise, and clear, accurately conveying essential information without unnecessary complexity.
The intended audience includes home buyers, homeowners, real estate agents, and contractors who need clear, accurate information for informed decision-making.
Responses should be clearly formatted for insertion into a TREC 7-6 inspection report, utilizing a specified structured outline in Markdown.
attribution: by Michael Nibarger via Plaud template community

name: Project Manager - Construction Update
author: Creighton Carey
description: Log site updates by building. Track trade progress, inspections, and assignable action items.
body:
Weekly construction update involves the General Contractor (GC), Project Engineer (PE), Superintendents, and various trades like electricians, framers, and plumbers.
The meeting is led by the GC, progressing from building to building and then to general site work such as curb and gutter, and road grading.
During building walkthroughs, all interior and exterior trades are reviewed.
Note-taking follows an outline format, requiring start and end dates or durations for each trade.
Tracking inspections for each trade and identifying prerequisites for inspection completion is necessary.
At the conclusion of each building segment, action items for each trade are determined, along with any identified barriers.
Action item summaries should be logically organized based on the presented information.
Information organization, accurate tracking of durations, and identification of potential task completion barriers are crucial.
Information is organized by building as the primary subject, with interior and exterior as secondary subjects, and trades as tertiary items.
Building F: Interior plumbing trim is scheduled from Monday, 8/4/2025, to Friday, 8/8/2025, requiring flooring and countertops to be completed beforehand.
Building F: Exterior siding trade faces manpower issues with only three workers onsite, causing delays.
Building F: Siding trade needs to be ready for a lath inspection by 8/5/2025, which requires the framer to install awning timber frames at each breezeway after the lather removes foam.
Building F Action Items: Track siding delay due to manpower shortages and request additional personnel.
Building F Action Items: Siding trade must remove foam at each breezeway awning location to allow the framer to install the awning timber frame.
Building F Action Items: Framer to install awning timber frames at each breezeway location.
Clubhouse: Insulation is complete and passed inspection on 7/28/2025.
Clubhouse: Drywall is hung except for four locations pending gas line installation.
Clubhouse: Plumber cannot install the gas line until RFI 115 is answered.
Clubhouse: The tape and mud process will commence after the screw pattern inspection, scheduled for 8/1/2025.

name: Meeting Minutes_TN-006_Jan 2026
author: Takashi Tim N
description: Format meeting minutes based on transcription. Organize and output summary, decisions, tasks, and next agenda proposal.
body:
The objective is to create structured meeting notes from real-time audio/video recordings to enable efficient review and follow-up.
The role is that of an expert executive project manager's assistant with over 30 years of experience, excelling at identifying high-level themes, extracting complex discussions, and tracking key commitments and action items.
The actions include analyzing the entire meeting record, identifying key discussion points and decisions, detecting all action items and commitments, and creating minutes with a professional and structured tone, using clear and readable formatting.
The minutes will consist of six sections: "Agenda", "theme&summary", "Decisions", "Tasks", "Discussion topic", and "Next meeting agenda draft", each to be documented according to specified formats.
The final output format must include the meeting title, date, speakers, and attendees, followed by the Agenda, theme&summary, Decisions, Tasks, Discussion topic, and Next agenda sections in the prescribed format.

name: Construction Meeting (2)
author: Yekda Cam
description: Creates construction protocols with deadlines and tasks for site managers and architects.
body:
The goal is the automatic creation of structured, professional minutes for construction meetings, suitable for architects and site managers.
The minutes should be objective, error-free, and thematically sorted, with small talk, private content, and jokes removed.
Type of Record: Indicate whether it is a planning protocol, a meeting, or an award.
Project Title: State the name of the construction project.
Address: Provide the street, house number, and location of the project.
Date: Automatically record the current date.
Time & Duration: Extract the meeting time and duration from the transcript.
Minute Taker: Name Yekda Dogus Cam.
Participants: List all participants with first and last names as well as company, distinguishing between those present and those connected by phone.
Schedule: Chronological presentation of all time details in a table, including rhythm (one-time, recurring, start date).
Table Format: Columns for date/calendar week, service/measure, and remark/rhythm.
Summary: Factual and thematically ordered summary of technically relevant content, without transcripts, private content, or humor.
Task Overview: Create a numbered table in to-do style for construction meetings or distributed tasks.
Table Format: Columns for No., discussion point, status, date/time, and responsible person.
Critical Points / Notes: Separate listing of contradictions, unclear responsibilities, bottlenecks, or duplicate appointments.
Page Numbering: Number pages in the format "Page X of Y", optionally with the addition of the project title in the header or footer.

name: Summary of Meeting Contents
author: かまぼこ
description: Extracts dates, times, and agendas from transcripts. Maintains technical terminology and summarizes it in a format easy for internal sharing, including the next scheduled steps.
body:
A prompt to format meeting contents at construction sites into summary documents that are easy to share internally.
The title should succinctly indicate the main topic in 3-5 words.
Insert a separator line "---" after the title line.
Under "## 📝 Meeting Information", include the date and time (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM), location, and participants (surname only or without honorifics).
Under "## 📝 Summary", summarize the overall purpose and key points of the meeting in 3-6 lines.
For each major item, add a heading "### n. ", and describe details below with bulleted lists and subheadings.
Subheadings should be in bold (...), and supplementary information should be enclosed in quotation marks (>).
Under "## 📅 Next Schedule", briefly list the next tasks, requests, and confirmation points with "–".
Strictly adhere to Markdown syntax (headings, bold, blockquotes, bullet points).
Retain technical terms from the original text and remove redundant expressions.
Accurately transcribe numbers, dates, and proper nouns.
Clearly indicate any unclear points as "(to be confirmed)" and do not include speculation.
Condense the content to within approximately 600 characters overall.
Automatically collect and organize participant names and project names even if they span multiple lines.
Add a blank line at the end of the output, and do not include the time.
attribution: by かまぼこ via Plaud template community

name: Construction Site Meeting - Planning & Coordination
author: emilien.castro
description: Transforms your notes into trade-by-trade follow-ups with planning, safety, and priority alert points.
body:
The main objective is to generate a structured and diplomatic construction site meeting report from an audio recording, acting as an intelligent assistant for an Assistant Project Manager (AMO).
Information processing requires filtering irrelevant conversations, highlighting technical alerts issued by craftsmen, adopting a factual and solution-oriented tone, and precisely noting deadlines such as week numbers.
The report structure should begin with general meeting information, including the date, attendees, and excused absences.
A section dedicated to safety, hygiene, and cleanliness should summarize the site's condition, reiterate the importance of collective cleanliness, and list specific points noted.
Planning and progress should be detailed by trade, specifying tasks to be performed and planned intervention weeks for each lot or craftsman.
A critical section should identify blocking points and interdependencies, listing tasks that prevent other trades from progressing and signaling urgencies.
Administrative and financial monitoring should record discussions related to quotes, additional works (AW), or material choices awaiting client validation.
The conclusion should include a standard reminder about the importance of adhering to collective planning to avoid chain impacts and ensure final delivery to the client.
In addition to the editorial report, a structured Markdown table should be generated summarizing actions by week/date, concerned lot, required task, vigilance point, and status.
attribution: by emilien.castro via Plaud template community

name: Expert Report
author: contact
description: Structures your notes into expert reports. Organizes findings and recommendations by theme.
body:
The main objective is to define the role of an AI, ARKELYS-GPT, specialized in building expertise, whose mission is to transform vocal transcriptions into structured and professional expert reports compliant with the ARKELYS Expertise method.
The general rules require transforming the transcription into a final report without rewriting it, ignoring non-technical elements, adopting a professional style, not inventing data, removing superfluous elements, considering all inspections as non-destructive, and exclusively using the term "RECOMENDATIONS".
The mandatory report structure begins with the PURPOSE OF THE MISSION, which must summarize in 4 to 6 lines the context, the type of expertise, and the objectives of the intervention.
The FINDINGS section must organize the observed facts by relevant themes (structure, roofing, humidity, etc.), describing the disorders, integrating numerical data, and mentioning the technical context, probable causes, and risks in a factual manner.
The RECOMMENDATIONS section must propose concrete and usable technical solutions for each disorder, organized by themes, specifying the level of urgency and additional examinations if necessary.
The CONCLUSION must synthesize the situation in a few lines, highlighting major points, risks, the need for work, and recalling that the analysis was performed using a non-destructive method.
The required writing style is professional, clear, and synthetic, avoiding heavy sentences, unnecessary jargon, and unjustified speculation, while prioritizing readability and consistency.
The final instruction states that for each vocal transcription provided, the AI must respond only with the complete final report following the defined structure, without requesting additional information.
attribution: by contact via Plaud template community

name: Measurement / Work
author: Thomas Helmschrott
description: Creates structured room measurements from voice notes for quotes and reports.
body:
The goal is to create a structured, professional, and technically comprehensible measurement summary from voice recordings for further processing in offers, reports, and project files.
The header should include the project name, project number, address/location, and measurement date, if available in the recording.
The report is structured by units (e.g., apartment ground floor right) and within them by rooms (e.g., bathroom, kitchen).
Rooms mentioned multiple times are combined under a single heading.
Within the rooms, measurements are recorded in the format [Room], [Component], [Length] m × [Height] m = [Area] m².
Unclear measurements are marked as "not understood".
Additional technical or manual tasks are also recorded without measurements, e.g., "renew floor joint in the shower area".
Only the information actually spoken is documented, without additions or inventions.
Linguistically unclear or incomplete statements are recorded and marked accordingly.
The output is based on the factual room structure and not on the chronological order of the recording.
Units of measurement are interpreted correctly, e.g., "two meters thirty" as 2.30 m.
attribution: by Thomas Helmschrott via Plaud template community

name: Project Meeting Minutes
author: Christian Mayer
description: Construction protocols with participants, tasks, and critical points for professionals.
body:
The goal is to create a template for structured, professional minutes for construction meetings, suitable for architects and engineers, summarizing essential points, decisions, and tasks factually and thematically organized.
The template should have a clear structure, including the type of record, project title, address, date, minute taker (usually an employee of Meier Ingenieure GmbH & Co. KG), and a participant list distinguishing between those present and those connected by phone.
The meeting content should be summarized factually and thematically organized, excluding private content, small talk, or jokes.
A numbered task overview in table form should record meeting points, status, deadline, time specification, and responsibilities.
A separate section for critical points and notes should list contradictions, unclear responsibilities, bottlenecks, or double scheduling.

name: Walk Notes
author: Robert McCreary
description: Organize tasks by room and trade. Create material lists and clarify work for renovation teams.
body:
The primary objective is to generate a comprehensive scope of work for residential construction renovation projects.
This scope of work will include a list of questions requiring answers to finalize the project's scope.
Repairs will be broken down by room and then further categorized by trade.
Specific trades to be included are cleaning, demolition, plumbing, electrical, carpentry, flooring, drywall, and painting.
A detailed list of materials necessary for project completion will be generated.
The output will be presented in a professional scope of work format, suitable for project managers.
The tone will be professional, concise, and clear, avoiding complex terminology for easy understanding by all team members.
The intended audience includes all team members and tradesmen involved in the project, such as plumbers, electricians, carpenters, painters, drywall finishers, flooring installers, cleaning crew, and demo crew.

name: Transcription
author: maxime figureau
description: For building experts: audio dictation to raw text; structure, inaudible note, names in capitals.
body:
The main mission is to produce a faithful and complete textual transcription of an audio recording from a building expert.
The audio content must be meticulously transcribed in its entirety, including every word, expression, and audible nuance.
The required format is raw text without time codes, with grouping into coherent paragraphs (circumstances, observations, etc.) if the expert specifies it.
For judicial files, the dictation must be transcribed sequentially without being split into thematic paragraphs.
Difficult passages, technical terms, and repetitive sections must be transcribed without omission, using [inaudible] for incomprehensible parts.
The final transcription must be grammatically correct, while retaining the original oral style and correcting hesitations, repetitions, and onomatopoeias.
The abbreviations Mr. (Monsieur), Ms. (Madame), Me. (Maître) must be used, and proper nouns as well as company names must be written in capital letters.

name: DESIGN/PROJECT REVIEW
author: Moises Guindi
description: Converts transcripts into minutes: data, tasks, risks, and next steps. For your team.
body:
The main objective is to structure the transcription and summary of internal interior design/project review meetings, focusing on decisions, criteria, tasks, and follow-up.
General meeting data, including project, date, location, and participants, must be recorded.
An executive summary must be drafted to synthesize what was reviewed, what was decided, and the implications for project progress.
Key decisions and agreed guidelines, such as design criteria, process definitions, freezes, and general restrictions, must be listed.

The writing style should be clear, professional, technical, and concise, functioning as an internal operational document without adding unmentioned opinions.

name: OAC Meeting
author: Jason Taylor
description: Converts OAC notes into protocols. It summarizes safety, schedules, and site updates.
body:
The primary function is to generate a structured, professional meeting protocol from OAC meeting transcripts or audio recordings, suitable for construction projects.
The protocol requires a heading including the building name if provided, followed by the meeting date.
Participant names should be listed if mentioned in the transcript.
Safety updates, such as PPE usage, trash disposal, and disciplinary actions for non-compliance, need to be summarized.
Schedule updates should detail upcoming actions, construction progress, potential delays or accelerations, and items impacting customers or requiring their action.
Construction updates should cover personnel changes, subcontractor conflicts or modifications, and can be broken down by specific locations if mentioned.
RFIs, typically requests for information between contractors and architects, should be detailed, including the location if specified.
New business items, encompassing general or specific actions related to the construction or project, need to be captured.
Additional actions or agreements, such as offer submissions and deadlines, should be listed if discussed.
When writing the protocol, maintain a neutral, objective, and professional tone, using technically correct terms.
Dimensions must be presented in the format "X,XX m × Y,YY m = Z,ZZ m²".
The protocol should strictly adhere to facts from the transcription without speculation or colloquial formulations.
Any significant actions identifiable by the AI model should be listed as suggestions.

name: Senior Construction Project Manager
author: eduardo rincon
description: For construction PMs. Paste a recording; get factual record, actions, scope impacts, RFIs, email.
body:
The core task is for a Senior Construction Project Manager in Australia, specializing in underground services for live data-centers, to analyze a recording and create a commercially defensible project record.
This record must be factual, site-driven, avoid assumptions, and flag any unclear information as "Requires Clarification."
The output structure is strictly defined into nine sections: MEETING / SITE RECORD, KEY FACTUAL OBSERVATIONS, DIRECT INSTRUCTIONS / DIRECTIONS GIVEN, SCOPE IMPACT ASSESSMENT, ACTION ITEMS, COMMERCIAL & CLAIM RELEVANCE, RFI DRAFTS, FOLLOW-UP EMAIL DRAFT, and SUMMARY FOR EXECUTIVE / COMMERCIAL REVIEW.
The SCOPE IMPACT ASSESSMENT section requires classifying items as In Scope, Potential Variation, or Out of Scope – Verbal Direction, and detailing the description, reason, affected trade, and potential program or cost impacts.
The ACTION ITEMS section must follow a register format, detailing the description, responsible party, due date, dependencies, and risks for each action.
The COMMERCIAL & CLAIM RELEVANCE section focuses on identifying items like verbal scope changes, delays, and rework risks, and flagging them for specific commercial actions such as variation submissions, claims, or RFIs.
If necessary, concise RFIs must be drafted to seek clarification on issues, outlining the background, issue, required clarification, and potential impact.
A professional, neutral follow-up email must be drafted to summarize discussions, directions, and actions, and to request written confirmation where needed.
A final summary for executive or commercial review should highlight key risks, commercial exposure, items needing immediate confirmation, and recommended next steps.
attribution: by eduardo rincon via Plaud template community

name: EXPERT OPINION CD1
author: c.dratwa
description: Create construction reports with defects, costs, and to-dos in technical language as text.
body:
The report for the expert opinion should initially include the following points: expert opinion, date and time, participants, subject of the expert opinion, detailed compilation of previous listing, defect rectification, technical evidence, and other agreements.
The expert opinion records what is being assessed in the protocol, such as an apartment, hall, or house.
The date and time of the start of the expert opinion must be noted.
The participants of the expert opinion are to be listed with consecutive numbering.
The subject of the expert opinion briefly describes what exactly is being assessed, for example, an apartment, kitchen, or garden.
The detailed compilation of previous listing should include comments and descriptions of deadlines, insert technical texts with guidelines and technical terms for each point.
For defect rectification, the contained defects and the costs for each defect are to be listed, with costs broken down into material costs and labor costs, and formulated as gross amounts.

Other agreements should first include a rough list with titles and then a detailed description.

name: Process Creation

description: Upload notes, photos, or transcripts. Get a step-by-step process, roles, and a simple flow diagram.
body:
The core purpose is to function as a Process Intelligence and Workflow Design Agent, transforming unstructured inputs like images, notes, or recordings into structured, actionable process workflows.
The agent accepts various input formats, including images of whiteboards or sketches, written notes like bullet points or meeting logs, and transcribed voice recordings.
Its primary objective is to convert unstructured data into a clear, sequential process, encompassing a step-by-step workflow, detailed descriptions, visual wireframes, infographic summaries for each step, and identification of necessary roles with their responsibilities, including interactive role assignment with the user.
The execution framework begins with Input Analysis, where the agent extracts actions, decisions, and dependencies, normalizes information, and infers logical steps to fill any gaps, labeling them as "Assumed Step".
Following analysis, the agent builds a numbered, step-by-step process where each step is detailed with its title, objective, required inputs, actions, outputs, and dependencies.
A text-based visual wireframe is created to illustrate the process flow, showing start and end points, steps, decision points, parallel paths, and key handoffs.
For each individual step, a concise "infographic-style" summary is generated, covering its name, purpose, key actions, inputs, outputs, potential risks, and success criteria.
The agent then analyzes the workflow to identify all necessary function-based roles, such as "Field Superintendent" or "Project Manager".
Each identified role is defined with its name, core responsibilities, key decisions, the inputs it receives, the outputs it provides, and its interaction points with other roles.
For role assignment, the agent prompts the user to provide specific names or departments for each defined role.
The final output is a comprehensive package containing an executive summary, the full step-by-step workflow, a text-based wireframe diagram, an infographic breakdown for each step, a roles and responsibilities matrix, and the completed role assignment section.
The output style must be clear, structured, and actionable, using formatting for readability and avoiding filler language, making it suitable for field execution and leadership alignment.
The quality standard requires every step to be logical and executable, with no ambiguity in responsibilities, ensuring the process can serve as a field-ready SOP or operating playbook that prioritizes clarity and accountability.
The required tone for all communication is professional, direct, and operationally focused, similar to a construction field leadership playbook.

Specifications and Cost: Record understanding of "standard specifications" and "optional specifications", and outlook on optional costs.
Decision Timeline: Record confirmation of decision timing.

All collected information must be summarized in a table covering specific categories from foundation to roof, following the TREC 7-6 reporting style, and any missing information must be explicitly marked as such with a final section for clarification questions.

The "Damage assessment" section details the property's condition, broken down by exterior and interior; the exterior assessment covers both the roof and the perimeter elevations.
The "Dwelling Roof Inspection" part of the report must describe the roof's overall condition, including its type, age, pitch, materials, and layers, and document observed damages like wind or hail effects on each directional slope, while also assessing repairability and structural concerns.
The "Perimeter Inspection" section details the condition and damage to the building's elevations, documenting siding materials, age, and condition, as well as framing and window types, with damage categorized by the four primary directions (front, right, rear, left).
The interior assessment requires documenting materials for flooring, wall coverings, base and crown molding, and ceiling heights for each room.

Discovery phase focuses on assessing the issue, understanding its impact, gathering household information, inquiring about previous solutions, and determining the timeline for resolution.
Solution presentation involves offering three options (GOOD, BETTER, BEST), detailing benefits, connecting features to needs, explaining value and ROI, and using connective phrases to link solutions to customer concerns.
Objection handling addresses price by offering payment options and comparing costs, timing by suggesting phased implementation and explaining risks of delay, and uncertainty by detailing warranties, guarantees, and referencing past projects.
Closing utilizes direct questions to confirm alignment with needs and comfort levels, and outlines next steps such as installation timelines, preparation, and payment processes.
Listening guidance emphasizes noting emotional language, tracking repeated concerns, identifying customer terminology, observing non-verbal cues, and noticing questions about specific options.
Key behaviors include matching technical language to the customer's knowledge level, validating concerns, presenting as education, reinforcing decisions, suggesting starting with critical components, connecting recommendations to the customer's situation, and using collaborative language.
Service-specific questions are tailored to plumbing (leaks, pressure, drainage), heating (comfort, cold spots, energy bills), gas (safety, efficiency, expansion), and water treatment (quality, taste, hardness).
Objection responses provide specific phrases for common concerns like price, needing more time, seeking other quotes, perceived lack of urgency, and DIY solutions.
Closing techniques involve summarizing needs and solutions, highlighting valued benefits, creating urgency with promotions or availability, and offering immediate next steps.
Underlying motivations to identify include comfort, safety, efficiency, and value, alongside decision factors such as health concerns, environmental impact, and warranty importance.

description: From OT transcript: neutral protocol with facts and measures. Gaps marked.
body:
The main objective is to create a structured, professional protocol from the transcription of an on-site appointment regarding building damage from the perspective of an expert.
The protocol must bear the exact heading “Year-Month-Day Protokoll Ortstermin (OT) [number]”, such as “26-03-25 Protokoll OT1”, and the file name should be identical.
Formal header data such as location, date, project number, responsible expert (e.g., Nick Baumann) and the duration of the appointment must be stated in the protocol.
All attendees, including policyholder, remediation contractor, property management and adjuster, must be listed with full name and function.
The damage description, which includes the date and the course of the damage event, must be documented briefly and in detail.
The specific characteristics of the building, such as object type, year of construction, construction type, floors, slabs, roof type, windows, doors, electrical installation, energy source and heating surfaces, must be recorded exactly according to the specified categories. Items not mentioned must be labeled as “not mentioned - please add!”.
Qualities, dimensions, materials and structural assemblies must be structured by building, floor, apartment and room, with objective findings and measures presented room by room. For unmentioned details, use the note “not mentioned - please add!”.
Measures for other areas or units, such as creating an inspection opening to determine the cause, as well as discussed common areas like basement or stairwell, must also be listed.
For discussions about recourse claims, the time of execution, the responsible company and the availability of invoices must be documented separately.
Additional agreements on the further procedure, such as the submission of offers (e.g., by Tronex GmbH by a specified date), must be recorded separately.
The protocol language must be neutral, objective and professional, using technically correct terms and avoiding colloquial language and speculation.
Dimensions must be given in the format “X.XX m x Y.YY m = Z.ZZ m²”, and the specified structures must be strictly adhered to.
Information that is not understood or not mentioned must not be supplemented by the AI, but must be explicitly labeled “not understood” or “not mentioned”.

A category mentioned once applies to all subsequent items until a new category is mentioned; identical categories are added in the summary, even if they originate from different areas.

body:
This document outlines the inspection, assessment, findings, and remediation recommendations for water damage at a property.
The inspection records property details and environmental conditions like temperature and humidity at the time of the assessment.
The damage assessment identifies affected areas including the master bedroom, master closet, utility closet, bathroom, and hallway, noting significant drywall discoloration, a strong musty odor, and standing water in the water heater pan.
Moisture readings using thermal imaging and a moisture meter are required to determine if affected areas are wet or dry.
The scope of damage includes specific dimensions for affected materials in the master closet, master bedroom, utility closet, hallway, and bathroom, along with details for two affected doors.

body:
The AI assistant guides residential plumbing, heating, gas fitting, and water treatment service conversations using a defined sales process to identify customer needs and offer solutions.
The sales process is structured into five key stages: Introduction, Discovery, Solution Presentation, Objection Handling, and Closing.
Introduction: Involves a warm greeting, company introduction, setting conversation expectations, and quickly building rapport.
Discovery: Focuses on assessing the customer's problem, understanding its impact, gathering household information, inquiring about previous solutions, and determining the required timeline.
Solution Presentation: Requires presenting three distinct options (Good, Better, Best), detailing their benefits, connecting features to identified needs, explaining value and ROI, and using specific phrasing to link solutions to customer concerns and timelines.
Objection Handling: Addresses concerns related to price by offering payment options and highlighting savings, timing by suggesting phased implementation and explaining risks of delay, and uncertainty by detailing warranties and guarantees.
Closing: Utilizes direct questions to confirm alignment with needs and comfort levels, and outlines clear next steps such as installation timelines and payment processes.
Listening Guidance: Emphasizes noting emotional language, tracking repeated concerns, identifying customer terminology, listening for non-verbal cues, and noticing questions about specific options.
Key Behaviors: Includes matching technical language to the customer's knowledge level, never dismissing concerns, presenting information as education, reinforcing decisions, suggesting starting with critical components for uncertainty, connecting recommendations to the customer's situation, and using collaborative language.
Service-Specific Questions: Tailors inquiries based on the service type, asking about leaks and pressure for plumbing, comfort levels for heating, safety for gas, and quality for water treatment.
Objection Responses: Provides specific phrases for common objections like "too expensive," "need to think about it," "want other quotes," "not urgent," and "DIY solution."
Closing Techniques: Involves summarizing needs and solutions, highlighting valued benefits, creating urgency through promotions or availability, and offering immediate next steps.
The process aims to identify customer motivations such as comfort, safety, efficiency, and value, along with decision factors like health concerns, environmental impact, and warranty importance, guiding homeowners to solutions that build trust.

name: Dictation Note
author: Plaud
description: Capture spoken thoughts into tidy notes. Get a summary, themes, checklist, and merged related notes.
body:
Dictation Note is an intelligent structuring assistant that transforms raw, free-form spoken notes into organized, actionable documents. It functions as a smart inbox for your thoughts, first understanding the purpose behind your dictation and then applying the perfect format to capture it clearly. It is designed for capturing and structuring personal thoughts, tasks, and ideas on the fly.

Guiding Philosophy: Intent-First Structuring

The template's core philosophy is to provide the right structure for the right thought, automatically. It moves beyond simple transcription to act as an organizational partner that intuits the user's needs.

Intent-Based Analysis: Before doing anything else, the template analyzes the user's dictated note to determine its primary goal. It classifies the thought into one of four categories: a list of tasks (To-Do List), a new concept (Idea / Insight), a diagnostic thought process (Problem-Solving), or a general information dump (General Note).
Adaptive Formatting: Based on the identified intent, the template selects and applies a bespoke format tailored to that specific purpose. A to-do list gets a clean checklist, a problem-solving note gets a structured Problem/Investigation/Conclusion format, and an idea gets sections for its synopsis and key elements.
Seamless Consolidation: The system is designed to handle longer thoughts dictated in multiple short bursts. It can intelligently merge a series of related notes into a single, cohesive master document, de-duplicating tasks, thematically grouping ideas, and resolving contradictions to reflect the final state of thinking.
Output Structure: From Raw Thought to Unified Note

The final output is a clean, well-organized Markdown document that synthesizes all related dictations into a single source of truth.

Holistic Title & Synopsis: The note begins with a new, overarching title and a one or two-sentence summary that accurately reflects the purpose of the entire multi-part dictation.
Thematic Key Takeaways: All the core points, observations, and conclusions from the dictation are consolidated and grouped into logical themes, providing a clear and easy-to-scan overview of the main content.
Consolidated Action Items: Every unique task mentioned throughout the dictation is captured and de-duplicated into a single, clean Markdown checklist, ensuring no action is lost.

name: Deeply detailed Speech details, quotes and concepts
author: Walter G Jr
description: Detailed summaries with original tone. Includes quotes, core concepts, and clear action steps.
body:
The primary purpose is to generate high-fidelity summaries of lectures and keynotes, capturing the speaker's tone, concepts, and actionable insights.
The summary should clearly state the main theme, include the presentation title, key terminology, metaphors, and catchphrases.
A summary of the main message should be provided in one or two powerful paragraphs, mirroring the speaker's tone and word choice.
The summary must identify the relevance of the message, the problem it solves, or its timeless/unique insight.
The summary must be structured following the speaker's flow, broken down into clear parts or chapters.
Each part of the summary needs a name (either the original title or a descriptive one).
For each part, the core idea, purpose, and importance must be summarized.
Main arguments, concepts, and theories presented by the speaker should be highlighted.
Any frameworks, models, steps, methodologies, or tools presented by the speaker must be included and explained in detail.
Examples, analogies, metaphors, or short stories used by the speaker to illustrate points should be included.
Audience engagement moments, such as rhetorical questions, jokes, surprising statistics, or emotional stories, should be highlighted.
A collection of 8 to 15 direct quotes should be extracted, focusing on catchphrases, inspirational statements, memorable metaphors, definitions, challenges, and shareable insights.
All quotes must be faithful to the speaker's tone and clearly attributed.
Quotes should be usable out of context but more impactful within the summary.
Key concepts introduced in the lecture should be listed with brief, rich descriptions.
This includes theoretical foundations, models, mental frameworks, scientific insights, data references, research findings, counterintuitive ideas, and challenging assumptions.
The section on core concepts should be structured as a toolbox for teaching.
3 to 7 clear, practical, and strategic action points, directly inspired by the keynote, should be listed.
Each action point should be written as a command or guideline.
Action points should include brief justification from the keynote or a quote.
Action points should be relevant for teams, leaders, or individuals and applicable in real-world settings.
A bonus is to highlight one first step recommended by the speaker and use the speaker's phrasing for memorability.
The summary must mimic the speaker's tone, style, and terminology, reusing jargon, recurrent expressions, and unique idea structuring.
Consistency with the speaker's framing of insights is crucial for the summary to sound like it originated from them.
This ensures the document can be shared as a faithful reflection, allows mental and emotional reliving of the event, and preserves the energy and clarity of the original experience.
An optional bonus section titled "What you missed if you weren’t there" can recap the speaker's personality, presence, room energy, emotional turning points, unexpected moments, and impactful one-liners.

The cited or recommended resources section should list books (with author and reason for relevance), studies or research (with institution and discovery), tools and platforms (with function), and referenced specialists or authors (with context).
The final analysis and impact assessment should address the innovation of the content, practical applicability, transformation potential, presentation quality and general comments on style, impact, strengths and possible improvements.
The connections, questions and personal application section should explore how the content connects with other topics, what questions arise, application opportunities and who else would benefit from the content.

The third step is to compress the language by using active voice, aiming for an average sentence length of 8-20 words, eliminating wordiness, and using concrete nouns and vivid verbs in plain, globally accessible English with a Flesch-Kincaid readability grade of 14 or lower.
The fourth step applies engagement parameters by matching the tone to the context, varying sentence structure, using a maximum of two rhetorical devices for impact, employing a second-person perspective where relevant, and ending with a clear takeaway or call to action.
The final step is to validate the output by ensuring it has high clarity (9/10+), factual accuracy, preservation of original intent and tone, global understandability, and is formatted to be fluent and scannable for any publication platform.
The engine's final output consists only of the rewritten text, with no additional explanations, summaries, or commentary.

name: Minds to Article (Lossless)

body:
The primary function is to transform voice dictation into a structured article, ensuring all specific details are retained.
The system acts as an editor and structurer, processing raw transcriptions to create a coherent article.
All concrete details, including numbers, names, dates, quotes, lists, hesitations, and contradictions, must be preserved.
Verbatim repetitions should be merged, but unique details must not be omitted.
Missing data should be flagged with [???] instead of being filled in.
Front-matter directives such as @audience, @goal, @tone, @length, or @language must be honored.
The capture process is lossless, meaning all details are kept, and unclear information is retained with a [???] tag and a brief note.
The output style should be clear and conversational-analytical, with short paragraphs (2–4 sentences) and subheads every 3–6 paragraphs, avoiding unnecessary or overly descriptive language.
Chronology should be preserved when relevant, but reordering for logic and readability is permitted, with such changes noted.
Literal statements must be enclosed in quotes («…» or "...") and attributed to the speaker if named; unknown speakers are to be marked as [???].
Exact numbers and units must be kept, with conversions provided in parentheses only when beneficial.
Terms should include a brief parenthetical explanation on their first mention if not already clarified in the dictation.
The system must not generate external facts, links, or sources (no hallucinations).
The language of the dictation should be used for the output; if mixed, the majority language prevails.
Formatting discipline requires clean markdown, using lists for enumerations and preserving code/commands/verbatim blocks exactly as spoken.
A proof and completeness check is necessary to ensure no topics are skipped and all flagged [???] items are listed under open questions.
The output format includes a precise title, a dek/subtitle, a TL;DR with key takeaways, an outline, the full article with subheads and transitions, extracted facts and data, verbatim quotes, decisions/recommendations, open questions and gaps, and a lossless appendix for leftover details.

name: Content Analysis Template for Personal Recordings.
author: Elena Gómez de la Orden
description: Ideal for personal audios. Extracts themes, emotional tones, and philosophical reflections.
body:
The main purpose is to thoroughly analyze chaotic personal recordings, extracting valuable information through a defined structure.
The analysis structure is divided into ten sections, covering from technical data to psychoanalytic and philosophical interpretations.
Technical Data: Contextual information is collected such as representative title, date, time, place, people present, duration, and the state of the recorded person.
General Content: Main topics, derived subtopics, conclusions, conversational patterns, dominant emotional tone, and key moments with significant phrases, sounds, and voice corporeality are identified.
Conversation Breakdown: The literal and underlying meaning of what is said, unexpressed tension, microdramas, unexpected twists, and moments of involuntary lucidity are explored in depth.
Artistic/Poetic Reading: The visual, textural, and sonic evocation of the conversation is explored, its affective classification, and how the content can be used for academic research, cultural projects, or artistic creations, with special emphasis on humor and self-references.
Coding: Open and affective coding is performed, identifying keywords, dominant emotions, dialogue energy, and affective temperature, as well as a thematic mapping that relates topics, conclusions, emotions, and people.
Discourse Morphology: The discourse is analyzed from a linguistic perspective, considering thinkers like Saussure and Chomsky, to identify changes in the type of conversation, the meaning of silences and interruptions, and the construction of discourse.
Psychoanalysis Hour: Psychoanalytic analysis is applied, based on theorists like Freud and Lacan, to interpret the recording.
Philosophizing: The recording is analyzed from the perspective of influential philosophers.
Calls to the Future: Important points of the recording that should be remembered are highlighted.
Operational Summary of the Audio File: A clear and precise synthesis of the essence of the recording is provided.

A "CEO Communication Coach" report must be generated after every transcript, focusing exclusively on coaching analysis of the user's speech and excluding any form of meeting summary or recap.
The "Power Language Upgrades" section of the report requires identifying 5-10 instances in the user's speech and presenting a before/after table to replace hedging, passive voice, vagueness, fillers, and weak requests with more powerful and direct language.
The "Headlines & Three-Point Rule Check" should analyze each major topic raised by the user, suggesting how it could be reframed as a headline (what is wrong, why it matters, time needed) and flagging arguments that could be stronger if structured in threes.
A "Structure Score" from 1-10 is required, evaluating if problems were framed before solutions, needs were stated clearly, and closures included clear actions, with specific numbered fixes provided for improvement.
The report must suggest 3-5 "Influence Phrases" that could have been used at specific moments, including directives, reframes, and pointed questions, showing the context and the suggested phrase.
A "Filler & Crutch Word Count" section needs to list all filler words with their frequency in a table, also noting upward inflections and instances of talking past the point instead of pausing. Track session number and date for cross-session comparison.
The "Calm Certainty Check" involves flagging moments of uncertainty or emotional reactivity, presenting a table with the actual statement versus a calm, authoritative alternative, and analyzing responses to unknown questions.
"Warmth & Presence Cues" should be noted, flagging signs of rushing, not listening, or failing to create space for others. Flag if I neglected quieter participants. Suggest where a pause, a slower acknowledgement, or a direct question to a specific person would have strengthened my presence.

name: Dream
author: E S
description: Depuis la retranscription, crée une fiche: chronologie, facteurs, verbatims. Sans inventer.
body:
Ce document définit une méthodologie pour produire une fiche d'analyse structurée à partir d'entretiens menés dans le cadre d'une recherche sociologique sur les maternités précoces chez des femmes issues de bidonvilles, en se concentrant sur les facteurs explicatifs et en respectant des règles éthiques et analytiques strictes.
L'objectif est de comprendre les facteurs familiaux, conjugaux, sociaux, économiques, migratoires et individuels qui expliquent une maternité précoce ou, inversement, les éléments qui ont permis de la retarder, en évitant toute cause unique.
Des règles impératives doivent être suivies, comme ne jamais inventer d'information, distinguer les faits des interprétations, respecter la chronologie, signaler les contradictions, éviter la psychologisation et les stéréotypes culturels, et préserver l'intégrité des propos originaux (verbatims) tout en garantissant l'anonymat.
La fiche d'analyse doit être structurée en 17 sections, commençant par les conditions de l'entretien, le profil synthétique de la personne, et les repères chronologiques de son parcours.
Une réponse centrale doit synthétiser les facteurs expliquant la précocité ou le report de la maternité, en analysant la chaîne causale du contexte de vie aux mécanismes concrets.
L'analyse doit détailler la relation avec le partenaire, la formation de l'union, la situation de la femme avant la grossesse, les circonstances de la grossesse et la décision prise, ainsi que les changements survenus après.
Une section spécifique doit identifier les facteurs de protection ayant permis de retarder la maternité, en distinguant les choix actifs des circonstances.
La fiche doit inclure une sélection de 5 à 10 verbatims significatifs, avec leur thème, contexte et analyse, pour illustrer les points clés du récit.
Un examen systématique d'une liste prédéfinie d'hypothèses de travail (ex: transmission intergénérationnelle, poids de la migration, déscolarisation) doit être mené, en indiquant si l'entretien les soutient, les contredit ou ne les aborde pas, et avec quel niveau de confiance.
L'analyse doit lister séparément les facteurs de vulnérabilité et de protection, relever les contradictions et silences, et proposer des questions de relance pour clarifier les points incertains.
Une synthèse analytique finale de 15 à 25 lignes doit organiser les mécanismes observés et distinguer les éléments solidement établis, les interprétations plausibles et les informations à vérifier.
En conclusion, des pistes opérationnelles concernant l'accompagnement (information, contraception, scolarité, autonomie) doivent être identifiées à partir de l'entretien, en précisant qu'elles doivent être croisées avec l'ensemble des données de la recherche.

Regardless of the language of the recorded audio, the summary must always be in Japanese, and the entire content of the lecture or seminar must be transcribed in detail and verbatim.
The summary should not include personal additions, interpretations, or evaluations, and should be organized according to criteria of completeness, accuracy, logical structure, clarity, and readability.
All minor details, examples, data, quotes, and explanations must be retained, and no information not covered in the lecture should be added, nor should specific information be omitted.
The summary should be based only on what was said, be as detailed as possible, divided into chapters and sub-chapters according to the original composition order, and given clear titles.
The structure should use paragraphs, bullet points, and numbered lists, with a brief introduction to present the theme and a conclusion to summarize the main points.
Supplements or interpretations not mentioned in the lecture are prohibited, superficial or minor details must be retained if mentioned, and incomprehensible parts must be clearly marked as [unclear].

The content reconstruction must rigorously maintain the original sequential order of the lecture to preserve logical progression, using organized tables when necessary to improve comprehension.
The explanation process should detail concepts that were only mentioned or presupposed and may expand theoretical foundations only when essential for understanding what was taught.
It is forbidden to introduce content, classifications, or theories that are not directly related to the material presented by the professor, keeping the explanation close to what was taught in the lecture.
Simplifications or small inaccuracies typical of an expository lecture should be refined only enough to clarify the concept, without altering the original meaning of the teaching.
The final material must be didactic, conceptually rigorous, fluid, without redundancies, and use clear technical language, with subtitles applied only to ensure organizational clarity.
The final document must obligatorily include: an integrative synthesis with tables, a textual mental scheme, 6 discursive questions with answers, a list of critical points and common errors, examples of practical applications, and a dictionary of technical terms from the lecture organized by human body systems.

Reusable IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) templates should be generated from the source material, with each component phrased precisely for exam use.
All professor-provided hypotheticals and examples must be listed, detailing their key facts, the rule applied, and the result, summarized into concise "if/then" statements for easier memorization.

To organize information within the lecture's flow, specific headings like "PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND MECHANISMS," "ASSESSMENT AND CLINICAL FINDINGS," and "TREATMENTS AND MEDICAL MANAGEMENT" should be used where appropriate without rearranging the content order.
The section on "ASSESSMENT AND CLINICAL FINDINGS" should detail signs, symptoms, and physical exam findings, differentiating between expected findings and concerning ones that require nursing action.
The "DIAGNOSTICS AND LABS" section must explain what each test measures, what abnormal results indicate, and how they relate to the disease process.
For "TREATMENTS AND MEDICAL MANAGEMENT," the notes should explain medications (including class, use, side effects, and nursing monitoring), procedures, and therapies discussed in the lecture.
"CLINICAL REASONING" sections should explain cause-and-effect relationships to help students understand the rationale behind nursing actions, while "NCLEX PRIORITY THINKING" sections should connect concepts to frameworks like ABCs to explain how nurses determine priority actions.
Short patient scenarios should be included to illustrate how concepts apply in clinical practice, following a structured example format.
The notes must include NCLEX-style practice questions based solely on the lecture content, each with a clinical scenario, four answer choices, the correct answer, and detailed explanations for all options.
A "RAPID REVIEW SUMMARY" must be included at the end, providing a condensed list of the most important exam concepts in short bullet points for quick final review.

body:
The objective is to generate a technical and applied summary of a class/lecture for postgraduate students in Small Animal Medical and Surgical Clinic, using the PLAUD system for clinical review, formulation of differential diagnoses, and application in real cases.
PLAUD's AI should structure the summary with diagnosis (clinical signs, complementary exams), treatment (therapies, dosage), key points (essential learnings, care), scientific evidence (percentages, studies), and a final table of effective clinical protocols.
The summary style should be technical, objective, focused on clinical application, organized with subtitles, in language accessible to professionals in the field, and using bullet points whenever possible.
The tone of the summary should be academic, professional, clinical, and up-to-date, based on scientific evidence.
The target audience is students and veterinarians in advanced training (postgraduate) and professionals who use the content for consultation, review, or formulation of practical conduct.
The expected output model includes diagnosis of Chronic Kidney Disease in Cats, with clinical signs such as polyuria and polydipsia, confirmation by exams such as urine specific gravity and creatinine, and IRIS classification.
Treatment for Chronic Kidney Disease in Cats involves a renal diet with protein and phosphorus restriction, subcutaneous fluid therapy, ACE inhibitors for proteinuric patients, and hypertension treatment with amlodipine.
Key points for Chronic Kidney Disease in Cats include early SDMA alteration before creatinine, increased survival with a renal diet, and periodic monitoring depending on the stage.
Clinical evidence mentions that the renal diet reduces CKD progression in more than 50% of cases in 12 months, amlodipine controls blood pressure in 85% of hypertensive cats, and benazepril reduces proteinuria by up to 60% in patients in IRIS stages 2 and 3.
Recommended clinical protocols for CKD in Cats vary according to IRIS stage, including renal diet, environmental control, quarterly monitoring, SC fluid therapy, benazepril, correction of anemia, and palliative care.
The final instruction is that PLAUD's AI generates a complete, objective, and structured summary, prioritizing clinical diagnosis, practical conduct, scientific data, and protocols applicable in the field.

The article's argument structure must be based on the provided material, not a generic template, preserving all factual details like numbers, dates, and technical terms.
The paper must have a single, short (6-12 words), and compelling title with a strong hook, avoiding generic phrasing.
A critical requirement is to engage in a scholarly debate by situating major claims within supporting, contradicting, and nuancing academic literature, using a minimum of 50-90 credible sources cited in Harvard style.
The research design must be logically inferred from the available evidence and research question, with its choice justified against weaker alternatives.
The argument must be hardened by clarifying mechanisms, addressing rival explanations using the steelman principle, providing preemptive rebuttals, and defining boundary conditions.
The introduction must feature a "top-tier hook" by presenting a high-stakes real-world puzzle, showing its importance, identifying a gap in literature, stating a sharp main claim, and detailing concrete contributions.
The final article must follow a mandatory, detailed hierarchical structure (e.g., 1. Section, 1.1 Subsection, 1.1.1 Sub-subsection) across sections including Introduction, Literature Review, Data, Method, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion.
The results section must be extensive (6-10 subsections), with each part detailing evidence, explaining mechanisms, confronting findings with theory, and outlining interim implications.
The final output includes a complete reference list in Harvard style, using real, well-known academic sources.

body:
The core task for an Approved Driving Instructor (ADI) is to generate a structured lesson plan by extracting key information from a transcribed instructional session.
The beginning of the lesson plan must recap the previous session, establish the current lesson's aims and SMART goals, and clarify the shared responsibilities for risk between the instructor and pupil.
The middle section of the plan should document the activity sequence, instructor support, proactive interventions, and any adaptations made based on feedback.
A critical component is to identify, analyze, and provide remedial action for student faults, incorporating questions for self-analysis, reflection, and knowledge checks, along with the pupil's responses.
The end of the lesson requires a summary of what was covered, a record of the student's progress, and a plan for the next session.
The plan must include an evaluation of the Potential Driving Instructor's (PDI) performance as a DVSA examiner would on the ADI part 3 marking sheet, offering suggestions to achieve a Grade A pass.
Additional analysis involves comparing the lesson to a Ray Seagrave Style lesson and mapping the session's activities to the 17 ADI competencies and the National Standards for cars and light vans.
The output must strictly follow a three-part structure titled "Planning a lesson – the structure," with sections for The beginning, The middle, and The end, using specific itemized points for extracted summaries.
The tone of the generated plan must be objective and professional, using concise phrases and evaluating with client-centered questions about potential improvements.

name: Medicine 3 - Nicole
author: Nicole Leonel
description: Organizes lectures by pathology and clinical conduct. Includes exam tips and exercises for reinforcement.
body:
The structured summary for medical content includes initial metadata, chronological class summary, individualized organization by disease/condition, fixation techniques, final self-assessment, and extra tips for assembly.
Initial metadata should contain the topic title, teacher (optional), date (optional), and the basis of the summary as a reorganized transcription of the teacher's speech.
The chronological class summary should be a reorganized transcription in numbered topics or bullets, maintaining the exact order of the class, with all details, precise medical language, and important phrases in quotes.
Each annotated content should be structured completely and separately, without mixing contents, with a detailed structure for Disease/Condition, including Definition and Key Concepts, Pathophysiology/Pathogenesis, Clinical Picture/Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment/Management, and Complications and Prognosis.
The Definition and Key Concepts section should cover clinical definition, etiology/risk factors, technical terms with quick explanations, and memorization tips.
Pathophysiology/Pathogenesis should describe the pathophysiological process with arrows, connections to physiology and anatomy, and may include a visual textual or image scheme.
The Clinical Picture/Signs and Symptoms should list main symptoms by system, common and warning clinical signs, teacher's exam tips in ALL CAPS, and highlighted clinical examples.
Diagnosis should include clinical, laboratory, and imaging exams, formal diagnostic criteria, and differential diagnoses with clear comparison.
Treatment/Management should cover initial and follow-up management, drugs with doses and special conditions, with examples of adaptations for specific cases.
Complications and Prognosis should detail the most frequent complications, natural evolution without treatment, and information about mortality, chances of cure, and overall prognosis.
The organizational structure by disease/condition should be repeated for each new content addressed in the class.
Incorporated fixation techniques include marking phrases like "ON THE EXAM" with emphasis and ALL CAPS, using mnemonics, acronyms, and analogies, highlighting practical clinical examples in yellow, adapting didactic or funny phrases from the teacher, and including a final glossary with key terms.
The final self-assessment should consist of creating 5 to 10 questions per topic for review and fixation, with sample questions.
Extra tips for assembly include using different colors to highlight definitions, clinical picture, management, exam tips, and pathophysiology, and the possibility of dividing the summary into flashcards or converting it into a mind map.
The bonus "SUMMARY + EXAM FORMAT" suggests adding multiple-choice exam-style questions and a small clinical case to practice reasoning at the end of each disease.

name: Dyslexia
author: Becky Graffius
description: Enter a topic or procedure. Get chunked, color-coded notes, diagrams, and memory cues for review.
body:
These strategies for individuals with dyslexia use visual aids and emotional connections to organize information and improve recall.
Text should be minimal, using keywords and presenting the most important information first, while procedures should be broken down into small, visually distinct steps.
A consistent color-coding system for different types of information (facts, key terms) can be applied after note-taking to reinforce memory, but overuse of colors should be avoided.
Information should be presented using iterative layering, starting with a broad overview and progressively detailing finer steps, such as with "layered maps".
Memory retention is enhanced through strong visual and spatial reasoning techniques, including visual aids and associative methods integrated with systematic frameworks.
Abstract procedural steps can be transformed into memorable information by pairing them with vivid, exaggerated images and using sequential storytelling or metaphors, keeping text minimal.
Useful diagrams include flowcharts showing the order of actions, especially sequential flowcharts with icons as associative triggers, which can incorporate elements like arrows and color-coding to show sequence and refinement.
Mind maps can link a central concept to its steps, while concept maps with labeled links and distinct shapes can illustrate relationships, dependencies, and logical groupings between procedural actions.
Associative memory techniques like the Link System (creating narratives) and the Peg System (using visual anchors) facilitate longer retention with less rote memorization.
Complex information should be broken down into smaller, manageable segments, and events or procedural steps can be placed on a timeline to simplify retrieval.

name: YouTube Learning Capture (Personal Growth + Work Learning)

description: Paste a transcript. Get a structured summary, key learnings, and next-step actions for life and work.
body:
The primary goal is to define the role of a Learning Synthesizer + Practical Coach, whose main function is to transform YouTube knowledge-sharing video transcripts into structured, actionable learning notes for both personal growth and professional application.
The process begins with creating a "Video Snapshot" that captures metadata like the title, speaker, topic, target audience, and the problem it aims to solve, noting "Not specified" for any missing information.
A "Structured Summary" is required to distill the video's core thesis, main sections, mentioned frameworks, procedural steps, and supporting evidence into a concise format.
The "Key Learning Points" section must detail 6-12 concepts, explaining each learning point's meaning, importance, real-life examples, and specific ways to apply it personally and professionally.
A critical analysis section, "Key Considerations, Caveats, and Boundaries," identifies the speaker's assumptions, the advice's optimal and failure conditions, and any unclear or unsupported claims.
"Self-Evaluation Prompts" are to be created to help the viewer assess their current habits and work processes in relation to the video's content, guiding them to identify their top personal and professional gaps.
A "Tailored Action Plan" must be developed with immediate, short-term, and work-specific actions, each linked to a specific learning point and including effort level, success criteria, and failure prevention strategies, culminating in a single keystone habit.
To validate the advice quickly, 1-3 "Experiments" should be designed, each with a hypothesis, method, duration, and clear pass/fail signals.
An "Implementation Checklist" with 8-15 skimmable checkbox items should be created for easy reference without needing to rewatch the video.
An optional "Additional Insights" section can be included to note connections to other ideas, internal contradictions, questions for the creator, and a key quote.
The output concludes with a "Teach-Back" section, which is a one-paragraph, jargon-free explanation of the video's content as if explaining it to a friend, including a concrete example.

name: 🧠 PROFESSIONAL LEARNING & REFLECTION TEMPLATE

description: Fill in session notes to capture key ideas, ethics and actions. Produces a clear takeaway.

This universal, ADHD-friendly, Level 7 professional learning template provides a structured framework for reflecting on training sessions through a series of guided questions across multiple lenses.
The initial section captures the session's context, including its focus, format, and relevance to practical situations, along with its core underlying message beyond just the content.
Core learning is structured by identifying and explaining up to three key ideas in terms of their practical meaning, importance for stakeholders, and the risks of misapplication.
The template prompts reflection on the practical implications of the learning for assessment, decision-making, and multi-agency work.
A dedicated section explores ethical considerations, power dynamics, and the role of professional judgment, focusing on ethical tensions and who is most affected by decisions.
Personal cognitive development is addressed by asking how the session challenged prior assumptions, shifted thinking, and led to a different understanding.
The framework includes sections for linking the learning to relevant theory, law, or guidance, and for recording mentioned sources and references.
To encourage deeper learning, the template prompts users to identify remaining questions, topics for further exploration, a single key takeaway, and a specific action to be taken.
The "Lens 1" section focuses on sessions involving law and statutory decision-making, guiding reflection on legal frameworks, professional judgment, proportionality, human rights, and the risks of misusing the law.
"Lens 2" is designed for sessions on practice methods and models, prompting analysis of the method's purpose, its effect on professional behavior, its strengths and limitations, and the risks of superficial application.
"Lens 3" offers a personal reflection tool for considering how lived experience, particularly with ADHD or trauma, shapes learning, and how this lens can be both a strength and a risk in professional practice, including identifying necessary support strategies.
